transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what brought you in to see me today?

Hi. Um... I guess I'm just having some issues getting through my work. I'm a teacher. And... I don't know, I'll sit down with a stack of essays or a curriculum document, fully intending to work, but... within ten minutes or so, I'll realize I've just been staring at the exact same page. 

My mind just wanders to three other things, and I'm... I'm barely taking in what's right in front of me. So... yeah. That's why I'm here.
Has this trouble concentrating been something you've noticed since childhood or your school years, or is this a new change that started more recently?

Um... I suppose it's not new. It's been going on since I was a kid. 

My parents used to find... well, just crumpled worksheets at the bottom of my backpack that I'd forgotten to hand in. And... my report cards back in primary school usually said I was bright but careless, or that I wouldn't finish my work unless someone was right there supervising me. So... yeah. It's been a while.

Aside from the concentration issues, do you notice yourself feeling restless, fidgety, or having trouble sitting still for long periods, or acting impulsively, like interrupting others or making quick decisions without thinking them through?

Um... no. Not really. I don't think I have trouble sitting still, or... anything like that. I'm usually pretty quiet, so I don't really interrupt people either. So... no. That doesn't really sound like me.
Over the past few weeks, have you noticed feeling persistently sad, anxious, or losing interest in things you used to enjoy?
Um... no. Not really. I mean... I guess I get frustrated with work sometimes, but... I don't think I feel sad or anxious. Just... normal, I suppose.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports chronic, pervasive inattentive symptoms (distractibility, difficulty sustaining attention on tasks, forgetfulness, incomplete work) that began in childhood, as evidenced by school reports of being 'bright but careless' and needing supervision to finish work. These symptoms persist into adulthood and impair occupational functioning (grading, curriculum work). No hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (fidgeting, restlessness, interrupting) are present, and mood/anxiety symptoms were explicitly denied, making primary mood or anxiety disorders less likely. The clinical picture is most consistent with Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, predominantly inattentive presentation, coded here as F90.0 per the given diagnostic framework.
